description: I’m a software engineering student (AI, C++, rocket dynamics) leading a team for the "Flame in Freefall" challenge. We are building an ML dashboard and RAG AI assistant to analyze NASA microgravity combustion data for spacecraft fire safety. I am handling the backend/ML. We are looking for a Frontend/UI Developer, a Data Scientist, and a Science Communicator. Join us to merge hard science with modern AI!
summary:
Flame in Freefall: Autonomous Microgravity Combustion Intelligence is an autonomous microgravity combustion intelligence and spacecraft fire-safety platform built on a Domain-Driven Clean Architecture.
It addresses the challenge by transforming over 12 Terabytes of NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) flight data across 24 investigations, 22 orbital drop-tower experiments, and 101 technical reports into actionable mission intelligence. The system delivers sub-2ms Gaussian Process predictive models with 90% conformal confidence bounds, an N-dimensional convex hull guard that strictly refuses ungrounded extrapolations, a live non-dimensional physics HUD and a real-time 60 FPS WebGL 3D flame simulator. For deep-space radio blackouts, an onboard circuit breaker and local FAISS vector index deliver 100% air-gapped, hallucination-free guidance backed by a mathematically calibrated refusal gate.
This platform is critical because fire in microgravity lacks natural buoyancy: still flames choke, but subtle cabin drafts (1–10 cm/s) trigger rapid, catastrophic spread—a hazard heightened in low-pressure, high-oxygen Artemis lunar and Mars habitats (56.5 kPa, 34% Oxygen) where traditional Earth (1g) fire standards fail. Beyond safeguarding astronauts, the platform advances civilian life-safety by tracking NASA spin-offs, including fine-water-mist extinguishers and lightweight composite firefighter air tanks.
details:
Flame in Freefall is an autonomous microgravity combustion intelligence and spacecraft fire-safety platform engineered to transform over 12 Terabytes of NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) flight telemetry, 22 orbital freefall drop-tower experiments, and 101 peer-reviewed NASA technical reports into real-time operational guidance. Operating on a Domain-Driven Clean Architecture (Hexagonal Ports & Adapters), the system works through five decoupled engines: a sub-2ms Gaussian Process Regressor providing 90% non-parametric conformal confidence intervals; an N-dimensional convex hull guard that mathematically refuses ungrounded extrapolations; a live non-dimensional physics HUD evaluating Péclet, Damköhler, Thermal Diffusivity, and Grashof numbers on the fly; a real-time 60 FPS WebGL/Three.js volumetric ray-marched 3D flame shader simulating zero-gravity spherical diffusion versus Earth-gravity buoyant plumes; and an onboard FAISS dense vector index with an automated Circuit Breaker that delivers 100% air-gapped extractive NASA guidance during deep-space radio blackouts.

The platform provides profound operational benefits by eliminating the dangerous blind spots of commercial AI models that hallucinate unsafe fire advice. It delivers immediate, unambiguous Go/No-Go flammability verdicts and normoxic equivalent pressure safety margins under NASA-STD-6001, enables 1-click simulation of critical mission hazards (such as Artemis habitat decompression, ventilation fan stoppage drafts, and structural heatsink barrier quenching), and automates the export of publication-ready flight readiness safety assessments stamped with cryptographic SHA-256 integrity signatures.

The intended impact of Flame in Freefall spans both deep-space human exploration and civilian life on Earth. In spaceflight, it directly safeguards astronaut crews aboard Artemis lunar bases and Mars transit vehicles against the lethal "Zero-Buoyancy Combustion Paradox"—where flames that appear to self-extinguish in still air explode into aggressive propagation when exposed to gentle cabin drafts of just 1 to 10 cm/s. On Earth, the platform accelerates civilian technology transfer by cataloging four verified NASA-derived life-safety technologies: fine-water-mist fire extinguishers replacing toxic Halon in commercial data centers, ultra-lightweight composite SCBA air tanks cutting firefighter cylinder weight by 40%(saving 13 lbs and preventing cardiac arrest), post-Apollo Project FIRES PBI turnout gear reducing municipal firefighter burn injuries by over 60%, and dust-discriminating smoke detectors preventing false alarms in transit tunnels and mines.

To develop the platform, I utilized Python 3.11 as the core language, Streamlit for responsive UI delivery, Three.js with custom GLSL ray-marching shaders for real-time 3D volumetric rendering, and Plotly for interactive conformal regression curves. Scientific computing and predictive modeling were built using Scikit-learn (Gaussian Process Regression with composite RBF and WhiteNoise kernels), NumPy, Pandas, and SciPy. Natural language retrieval and air-gapped flight autonomy were powered by FAISS vector indexing, fastembed with BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 384-dimensional embeddings, and LangChain document chunking. DevOps, quality assurance, and testing were executed using Pytest(100% pass rate across 27 automated suites), Docker for multi-stage container deployment, and Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) for headless end-to-end verification.

The creativity of my project lies in merging rigorous transport scaling physics with cinematic, interactive visualization and deterministic safety engineering. Rather than treating microgravity fire as an abstract number or a static plot, I unified real-time mathematical scaling with a 60 FPS volumetric shader that shifts luminescent color and geometry as users adjust atmospheric parameters. Furthermore, I solved the life-critical challenge of AI safety in space by introducing a mathematically calibrated cosine similarity refusal gate and an air-gapped Comm Blackout Mode, ensuring the system strictly refuses to extrapolate when queried outside validated envelopes and provides honest NASA evidence gap analysis instead.

Throughout development, I prioritized four core factors: human-system safety and scientific honesty (strictly refusing to fabricate predictions for untested lunar atmospheres), deterministic air-gapped flight autonomy (ensuring sub-2ms latency, a 394 MB RAM footprint, and zero cloud dependencies for deep-space missions), rigorous compliance with spaceflight standards (implementing NASA-STD-3001 and WCAG AAA dual-channel accessibility using geometric symbols ●, ▲, and ■ paired with color), and verifiable data provenance (linking every claim to primary NASA NTRS citations with cryptographic hash integrity).
